sections.text: To estimate a renovation accurately, build the budget from the bottom up: measure the job, work out quantities for each material, multiply by a unit price you have confirmed with local suppliers or written quotes, add labor and permits, then add a separate contingency for surprises. A single per-room price from an article is only a starting point, because costs vary widely by location, finish level and the condition of the existing house.
Why do renovations go over budget?

The usual causes are all estimation gaps rather than bad luck: quantities guessed instead of measured, materials priced before the product was chosen, labor left as one vague number, and nothing set aside for what is behind the walls. Scope creep adds to it, since each upgrade chosen mid-project is priced on the spot and without comparison.
What does a bottom-up estimate look like?

Take a 12 ft by 14 ft kitchen with 8 ft ceilings, a 3 ft by 7 ft door, a 3 ft by 5 ft window and a 20 ft counter run. Quantities come from measurements, and the unit prices below are made-up placeholders for illustration only; replace every one with a local quote.

rows: 380 sq ft of wall x 2 = 760 sq ft; at an assumed 350 sq ft per gallon that is 2.17, so buy 3 gallons
20 ft x 1.5 ft = 30 sq ft + 10% = 33 sq ft

sections.text: The wall area is the perimeter times the height, minus openings: 2 x (12 + 14) x 8 = 416 sq ft, less 21 sq ft for the door and 15 sq ft for the window, gives 380 sq ft. Paint coverage per gallon depends on the product, so use the figure on the can you actually buy. Appliances, plumbing, electrical and demolition are left out of this example, and in a real project you would add them or exclude them on purpose.

The mix matters more than the total. In this example the cabinet and countertop allowances are 65.5% of the subtotal, labor is 21.8%, and the flooring, paint and tile you can measure precisely are only about 10.5% (6.7%, 0.9% and 2.9%). That means your estimate is only as good as your allowances, so firm them up first.
How big should the contingency be?

There is no universal rule, and the right size depends on how much is unknown. A cosmetic update on a recently built home has few unknowns; opening walls in an older house has many. Many planners set aside a separate percentage of the subtotal and keep it out of the scope. The table shows 10%, 15% and 20% on the example subtotal as illustrations.

Now test it. Suppose opening the floor reveals a damaged subfloor that costs an extra $2,500 to repair (a made-up figure). A 10% contingency of $1,374 would not cover it; 15% at $2,061 would not either; 20% at $2,748 would. A labor overrun is smaller: if the 60 hours of labor run 25% long, that adds $750, or 5.5% of the subtotal. Material allowances are the bigger risk, since a 20% jump in everything except labor and permits adds about $2,088, or 15.2% of the subtotal.

If you borrow part of the cost, the interest is a cost of the renovation too. As an assumption only, borrowing $20,000 at 9% annual interest over 60 months gives a payment of about $415.17 a month and total repayments of about $24,910, which is $4,910 of interest. Your own rate, term and fees will differ, so get actual offers and compare the total repaid, not only the monthly payment.
Where to look for savings, and what to protect

items: Compare at least three itemized written quotes for the same scope, so differences are visible line by line.
Decide the finishes before the work starts. Changes made mid-project are the easiest way to overspend.
Doing simple work yourself, such as painting, shifts cost from labor to your time, but only if you can do it well.
Be cautious about cutting corners on plumbing, electrical, structure and waterproofing, where mistakes are expensive to reverse.
Keep the contingency separate from the scope, and record what you spend from it.

sections.text: Often, for structural, electrical, plumbing and some other work, but the rules differ by location and by the type of work. Ask your local building department before you commit to a plan. Unpermitted work may create problems when selling the home or making an insurance claim in some places, and licensed trades will know what applies locally.

All unit costs, allowances and the interest rate in this article are illustrative assumptions, not market data. The quantities and totals were calculated from those assumptions with a script and rounded to the nearest dollar.
